children.text: Eight days is not enough to see all of Egypt. As a first trip, it is strong. Linking
Cairo
Giza
Aswan
, and
Luxor
correctly opens up the large flow of ancient Egypt.
Eight days in Egypt is not a short trip.
Of course it is not enough to see the whole country. Adding
Alexandria

, the Western Desert, the Sinai, the Red Sea, Minya, and Fayoum all quickly breaks the schedule. As a first trip to Egypt built around Cairo, Giza, Aswan, and Luxor, eight days is more than enough time to mean something.
The key is not to break the thread of the trip.

This itinerary connects the pyramids, the museum, the Nile, the southern temples, and the east and west banks of Luxor. It leaves the Red Sea holidays and Sinai detours out. Those are good trips on their own; in an eight-day first visit, they blur the focus.
What this is shaped for is not a wide-and-shallow Egypt. It is a readable arc — from the Old Kingdom to the New Kingdom, from Cairo to the southern Nile, on to the
Valley of the Kings
What to decide before you go
In an eight-day trip, the choice of how to move matters.

From Aswan to Luxor, the options are a Nile cruise, a dahabiya, road, train, or a domestic flight. A cruise combines movement and lodging and is the most legible option for a first visitor. A dahabiya is quieter, and it is a trip about the river itself. A hotel-based plan using cars or flights is more flexible, but more demanding to organise.

The handling of the Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) — which opened formally on 1 November 2025 — also changes the shape of the itinerary. To see the complete Tutankhamun collection and Khufu's solar boat, give the GEM at least half a day. The old Egyptian Museum on Tahrir Square is still valuable, but on a first visit choosing one, the GEM is now the centre.
Day 1: Arrive in Cairo
Don't push the first day.

From Cairo International Airport to your hotel in the city or near Giza, the trip takes anywhere from thirty minutes to over an hour depending on traffic. Adding a heavy site visit on arrival sends fatigue into the following days.

This is a day to check in, eat somewhere nearby, and let the body learn the speed of the city. Where you stay — Zamalek, Garden City, downtown, or the Giza side — changes the first impression of Cairo considerably.
Cairo is not a city to try to understand on day one. It is a city to accept first.
Day 2: Giza and the Grand Egyptian Museum
On day two, start at Giza.
Khufu, Khafre, Menkaure,
the Great Sphinx
, the surrounding cemeteries.
The Giza plateau
is larger and more complex than the photographs suggest. If you can, arrive early. The light is softer and the crowds are still thin.

To enter the Great Pyramid you need a separate ticket. The interior is narrow, warm, and undecorated. As an experience of being inside an enormous structure, it is still distinctive. It is not for anyone uncomfortable in tight spaces.

In the afternoon, move to the GEM. It sits near the Giza plateau, so combining the two on the same day is straightforward — but doing both in any depth in one day is not easy. At the GEM, prioritise the Tutankhamun galleries, Khufu's solar boat, and the Old Kingdom sculpture.
This is the Old Kingdom and museum day. Don't push the evening; an earlier night carries into day three.
Day 3: Saqqara, Memphis, and Islamic Cairo
Day three is for what came before Giza and another layer of Cairo.

Djoser's step pyramid at Saqqara is one of the turning points of Egyptian monumental stone architecture. Looking only at the finished pyramids at Giza, you do not see the developmental process of the royal tomb — at Saqqara, you do.

Saqqara is not only the step pyramid. There are Old Kingdom mastaba tombs and tombs from later periods. The walls — daily life, agriculture, hunting, craft — show an ancient Egypt very different from the colossal royal monuments.
Memphis was once the capital of unified Egypt. The visible remains are limited, but through the colossus of Ramses II and the alabaster sphinx you can feel the trace of an ancient city.
In the afternoon, Islamic Cairo. Walking around al-Azhar, al-Muizz Street, the Mosque of Sultan Hasan, the Citadel, and part of
Khan el-Khalili
shows that Egypt is not built only from antiquity. Don't try to cover everything. One or two places, looked at carefully, work better.
Day 4: Fly to Aswan
Cairo to Aswan, about a 90-minute flight.
When you arrive in Aswan, the speed of the trip changes. You leave the density of Cairo and step into a southern town where the Nile looks wide and quiet.

In the afternoon, Philae is the priority. The temple of Isis was threatened by flooding after the construction of the old Aswan Dam and was moved to its present location on Agilkia Island. The boat approach to the island is part of what makes Philae particular.
If there is time, add
the Unfinished Obelisk

or the High Dam. The Unfinished Obelisk shows a piece of ancient stone-quarrying work that was abandoned mid-cut. The High Dam is less a beauty spot than a way to read how modern Egypt managed the Nile in the twentieth century.
For the evening, take a felucca on the Nile, or walk the Corniche.
Day 5:
Abu Simbel
, or Aswan in depth
Day five sets the character of the trip.

For Abu Simbel, the start is early. The Great Temple of Ramses II and the small temple for Nefertari are among the most powerful pieces of monumental Egypt. The modern story matters too: in the 1960s, to save the temples from rising Lake Nasser, they were cut apart and rebuilt on higher ground.
The drive is long. As a day trip from Aswan, you leave very early and return between midday and afternoon.
If you keep Abu Simbel out, the alternative is to go deeper into Aswan.
The Nubian Museum
Elephantine Island
, a Nubian village, Kitchener's Island, a longer felucca sail. Aswan is not only big monuments; it is a town for being in the river's time.
Which is correct depends on the goal of the trip. For the force of the monument, Abu Simbel. To hold on to Aswan's air, give the day to the town.
In the evening or the next morning, move on to Luxor. If you are taking a cruise, this part is replaced by the boat trip.
Day 6: Luxor east bank
In Luxor, start with the east bank.

Karnak is a place to visit early. It is not a single temple but an enormous religious precinct that was built and added to for almost two thousand years. The 134 columns of the Great Hypostyle Hall are famous, but Karnak's value is not only its scale. Kingship, the priesthood, festivals, and the memory of earlier kings all sit layered on top of each other.
Allow at least two hours; three is better. Rushing through leaves you with only "the place with the big columns."
In the afternoon,
the Luxor Museum
is a strong addition to the east-bank day. The scale is modest, but the displays are well-curated, and they hold important sculpture and material from around Luxor.

In the evening, Luxor Temple. The night lighting suits the temple well. Karnak and Luxor Temple were once linked by the avenue of sphinxes. Reading them not as separate sites but as parts of one festival map changes the meaning of the east bank.
Day 7: Luxor west bank
Day seven is the west bank.

Go to the Valley of the Kings as early as possible. The standard ticket admits you to several tombs, but which tombs are open changes with the season. There are also additional-ticket tombs. The tomb of Seti I (KV17) is expensive, but it is a very strong choice for decoration quality and scale. The tomb of Ramses V and VI (KV9) is another with strong impact — the astronomical ceiling and the interior space carry weight.

The tomb of Tutankhamun is small and only modestly decorated, but it is bound to the story of the 1922 discovery, so for many it is worth entering. After seeing the Tutankhamun treasures at the GEM, how you place the tomb itself becomes a personal call.

After the Valley of the Kings, the mortuary temple of Hatshepsut. The three terraces rising into the cliff are a form unlike anything else in Egyptian architecture. If time allows, add the Colossi of Memnon, Medinet Habu, or the Ramesseum.

Don't overload the west bank. The tombs and the mortuary temples are information-heavy, and the heat presses in. Two or three sites looked at carefully stay with you longer than five visited at speed.
Day 8: Back to Cairo, or depart
The final day is for the trip back to Cairo or a direct international connection.
If you have a little morning time, you can pick up a Luxor site you missed. On flight days, don't load the morning too heavily.

If Cairo gives you the afternoon, you have choices — the Egyptian Museum on Tahrir, Coptic Cairo, or a lighter time in Zamalek. Closing the trip with one more huge site is not always the right move; using the time to absorb what you've already seen is just as good.
What this itinerary shows you
These eight days do not show you all of Egypt.
They do show you the large line of ancient Egypt.

At Saqqara and Giza, the beginning of royal tombs and monumental stone. At Aswan, the southern Nile, the cult of Isis, the dam, the modern story of preservation. At Luxor, New Kingdom kingship, the temples, the funerary world of the Valley of the Kings. At the GEM, how those objects are being told again in modern Egypt.
These are not separate checkboxes.
How is a king remembered? What is a temple built for? Why was a tomb hidden? How did the Nile shape the country? An eight-day trip lets these questions begin to link up.
Practical notes
October through April is the easier season. December and January are crowded. May to September is hot — in Luxor and Aswan the schedule has to be built around the early morning.
Domestic flights connect Cairo, Aswan, and Luxor efficiently. With transfers and wait time, a flight day still costs you half a day. Don't plan by air time alone.

A guide is not necessary every day. At Giza, Saqqara, Karnak, and the Valley of the Kings, however, a good Egyptologist guide changes how much you understand. On a short eight-day trip, a good guide also saves you the time of finding your way on the ground.

Don't underestimate the heat or the fatigue. Egyptian sites are large, shade is limited, and there is a lot of movement. The most stable design puts the heavy visits in the morning, rests at midday, and moves again in the late afternoon.
Is eight days enough?
Eight days is not long enough to finish understanding Egypt.
As a first trip, it is enough. See the pyramids, feel the Nile move south, walk inside the temples, go down into the tombs of kings. With that much done, Egypt stops being a set of famous sites.
What should remain at the end of this trip is not the sense of "done."
It is the sense of "now I know what to look at next."
That is the best ending for an eight-day Egypt trip.

deck: Eight days is enough to link Cairo, Giza, Aswan, and Luxor without strain, and to see the pyramids, the Nile, and the Valley of the Kings as one connected line.
